pages.title: Teaching a language model to see
pages.subtitle: What problem LLaVA solves and why it mattered in 2023

blocks.html: By early 2023, two revolutions had happened separately. Instruction tuning turned raw language models into helpful assistants: you fine-tune GPT on (instruction, response) pairs and suddenly it follows arbitrary requests like "summarize this" or "write code for X". Meanwhile, vision-language models like CLIP had learned to align images and text, but they were not chatbots. You could ask CLIP "is this a cat or a dog?" only by a rigid matching procedure. Nobody had a model you could simply talk to about an image.

The gap LLaVA closes: there was no large-scale dataset of multimodal instruction-following data, because such data is expensive and ill-defined to collect by hand. How do you crowdsource "have a thoughtful conversation about this photo"? The paper's core trick is to sidestep human annotation entirely and use a language-only GPT-4 to generate the multimodal training data, then connect a frozen vision encoder to an LLM with a single trainable layer.

We present the first attempt to use language-only GPT-4 to generate multimodal language-image instruction-following data. By instruction tuning on such generated data, we introduce LLaVA: Large Language and Vision Assistant, an end-to-end trained large multimodal model that connects a vision encoder and an LLM for general-purpose visual and language understanding.

The name spells out the whole architecture: Large Language and Vision Assistant. Three headline results frame the paper. (1) On a synthetic multimodal chat benchmark, LLaVA reaches a 85.1% relative score versus text-only GPT-4 acting as a teacher. (2) When LLaVA and GPT-4 are combined, they set a new state of the art on the ScienceQA science-question benchmark at 92.53% accuracy. (3) The whole recipe is cheap: the instruction data is generated by an API, and training the connector is fast.

Why this was a landmark. LLaVA showed that you do not need to train a giant multimodal model from scratch (the GPT-4V / Flamingo / GPT-4 path). You can bolt vision onto an existing open LLM (Vicuna) through one tiny projection layer, teach it with machine-generated conversations, and get a model that genuinely chats about images. It made multimodal assistants reproducible on an academic budget and kicked off a wave of open VLMs (LLaVA-1.5, MiniGPT-4, Qwen-VL, and many others).

pages.title: Turning captions into conversations with GPT-4
pages.subtitle: How a blind language model writes training data about images

blocks.html: Here is the chicken-and-egg problem. To instruction-tune a model that talks about images, you need examples of people talking about images. But GPT-4 (the only model smart enough to write good conversations in 2023) cannot see images. The clever move: feed GPT-4 a textual description of the image so it can reason about the scene as if it could see it.

Every image in the COCO dataset already ships with two kinds of text annotation: captions (five short sentences describing the scene, e.g. "A group of people standing outside of a black vehicle") and bounding boxes (each object plus its location, e.g. person: [0.681, 0.242, 0.774, 0.694]). Together these give GPT-4 a surprisingly complete symbolic picture: what is in the scene and roughly where. The authors call this the model's "eyes" made of words.
From this textual scene, the authors prompt GPT-4 to produce three distinct response types, designed so the trained model learns different skills:

items: Conversation — a multi-turn Q&A between an imagined person and the assistant about the photo: object types, counts, actions, locations, relative positions. Teaches grounded back-and-forth dialogue.
Detailed description — a rich, paragraph-length account of the whole scene. Teaches the model to produce thorough, comprehensive descriptions on demand.

Complex reasoning — questions that require inference beyond what is literally visible, e.g. "What challenges might these people face?" given a photo of luggage on a car. Teaches step-by-step reasoning grounded in the image.

blocks.html: In total the pipeline produces 158K unique language-image instruction samples: 58K conversations, 23K detailed descriptions, and 77K complex-reasoning examples. A handful of hand-written seed examples are given to GPT-4 as in-context demonstrations to fix the format and quality, then the rest is generated at scale.

Why use both captions and boxes? Captions alone tell GPT-4 what is in the scene but not where or how many. Boxes add spatial grounding so the generated conversations can correctly answer "how many cars?" or "what is to the left of the person?". Feeding both makes the synthetic dialogue spatially faithful, which is exactly the skill a visual assistant needs. This is also a neat instance of distillation: a strong text model teaches a multimodal model a capability the teacher itself lacks (it cannot actually see).

pages.title: One matrix bridges vision and language
pages.subtitle: CLIP encoder + projection + Vicuna LLM

blocks.html: The architecture is almost shockingly simple, and that simplicity is the point. You already have a great vision encoder (CLIP ViT-L/14, which knows how to turn an image into rich features) and a great language model (Vicuna, an open chat-tuned LLaMA). They speak different languages: the vision encoder emits image feature vectors, the LLM consumes word-embedding tokens. LLaVA's only job is to build a translator between the two.

The analogy: imagine the LLM only understands English words, and the vision encoder hands it documents written in a foreign alphabet. Rather than retrain either expert, you hire one interpreter who maps each foreign symbol to an English word the LLM already understands. That interpreter is a single linear layer, the projection matrix $\mathbf{W}$.

Given an input image $\mathbf{X}_v$, the frozen CLIP encoder $g(\cdot)$ produces a grid of visual features $\mathbf{Z}_v = g(\mathbf{X}_v)$. A trainable projection matrix $\mathbf{W}$ then maps those features into the LLM's word-embedding space:

Reading it term by term: $\mathbf{X}_v$ is the raw input image. $g(\cdot)$ is the frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 vision encoder; the paper uses the features from the layer just before the last. $\mathbf{Z}_v$ is the resulting grid of visual feature vectors (each patch of the image becomes one vector). $\mathbf{W}$ is the only newly trained component here, a linear projection matrix. $\mathbf{H}_v$ is the output: a sequence of visual tokens living in exactly the same embedding space as the LLM's word tokens, so the language model can attend to them as if they were words. The image has been turned into a short "sentence" the LLM can read.

Why just a linear layer? It is the lightest, fastest bridge that works, and it keeps the experiment honest: if a single matrix suffices, the heavy lifting is already done by CLIP and Vicuna. The authors explicitly note that more sophisticated connectors (the gated cross-attention of Flamingo, or the Q-Former of BLIP-2) are possible and left as future work. The follow-up LLaVA-1.5 indeed swapped this single matrix for a small two-layer MLP and gained accuracy, validating that the linear layer was the minimal-but-not-final choice.

What stays frozen. During the first stage, both CLIP and Vicuna are frozen and only $\mathbf{W}$ trains. This is what makes LLaVA cheap: you are fitting one matrix to align two pre-trained giants, not retraining billions of parameters. It echoes the lesson of adapters and LoRA from the NLP world: freeze the expensive backbones, train a tiny bridge.

pages.title: The autoregressive objective
pages.subtitle: How the model learns to answer, token by token

blocks.html: Now that the image is a sequence of visual tokens $\mathbf{H}_v$ sitting in the LLM's vocabulary space, training is just ordinary language modeling. For each image the authors build a multi-turn conversation $(\mathbf{X}_q^1, \mathbf{X}_a^1, \dots, \mathbf{X}_q^T, \mathbf{X}_a^T)$ of $T$ turns, treating all the model's answers $\mathbf{X}_a$ as the text to predict, and everything else (the image and the human's questions) as the context to condition on.

Concrete example. The prompt fed to the model is literally: [visual tokens from the photo] + "How many cars are in the image?" The model must then emit "There are two cars." one token at a time. The loss only counts the assistant's tokens; the image tokens and the question are given for free, never predicted.
For a sequence of length $L$, the probability the model assigns to the target answer tokens is the product over positions:

Term by term: $\mathbf{X}_a$ is the target answer (the tokens we want the model to produce). $\mathbf{X}_v$ is the image, present in every factor because every answer token may depend on the picture. $\mathbf{X}_{\text{instruct}}$ is the instruction/question text. $L$ is the number of answer tokens. $x_i$ is the $i$-th answer token. The subscript ${autoregressive left-to-right factorization. $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ are the trainable parameters. Maximizing this likelihood is equivalent to minimizing the usual cross-entropy (next-token) loss over the answer spans.

items: Stage 1 — feature alignment pre-training. Freeze CLIP and Vicuna; train only the projection $\mathbf{W}$. The data is 595K image-caption pairs reframed as simple single-turn instructions ("Describe the image" -> caption). This teaches the visual tokens to land in the right spot of the LLM's word space, like aligning the interpreter's dictionary.

Stage 2 — end-to-end instruction tuning. Keep CLIP frozen, but now train both $\mathbf{W}$ and the Vicuna weights on the 158K GPT-4-generated instruction data. This teaches the model to actually hold conversations, describe in detail, and reason. Two models are reported: a general multimodal chatbot, and a ScienceQA-specialized variant.

blocks.html: Why two stages and not one? If you jumped straight to fine-tuning the LLM while the projection is still random, the visual tokens would be noise and the LLM would learn to ignore them, or its language skills would get corrupted chasing garbage signals. Stage 1 cheaply gets the bridge roughly right first; stage 2 then teaches behavior without destabilizing the alignment. This curriculum mirrors how BLIP-2 also separates representation alignment from instruction following.

pages.title: Judging an open multimodal chatbot
pages.subtitle: Using GPT-4 as the grader, and what LLaVA gets right

blocks.html: How do you score open-ended visual chat? There is no single right answer to "have a thoughtful conversation about this photo". The authors borrow a now-standard trick: use GPT-4 as an automatic judge. For each test image they have the (text-only) GPT-4 read the ground-truth captions and boxes, produce a reference answer, and then score LLaVA's answer against it on a 1-10 scale for helpfulness, relevance, accuracy, and detail. The reported metric is LLaVA's score as a percentage of GPT-4's own reference score.

On the LLaVA-Bench (COCO) set of 30 images with 90 questions, the full recipe scores a relative 85.1%. The ablation is the interesting part: training on all three data types (conversation + detailed + reasoning) clearly beats any single type, confirming that the three flavors of generated data each contribute a distinct skill. Adding the complex-reasoning data in particular gives a large jump in the model's ability to reason about the scene rather than just describe it.

On the harder LLaVA-Bench (In-the-Wild) set, deliberately built from challenging real-world images (memes, paintings, dense scenes) with detailed manual annotations, LLaVA shows strong but imperfect performance, exposing limits in fine-grained recognition and OCR-heavy images, the exact weaknesses LLaVA-1.5 later targeted.

blocks.text: Two anecdotes that show what it learned

blocks.html: The "extreme ironing" example. Shown a man ironing clothes on the back of a moving taxi, LLaVA correctly identifies the unusual, humorous situation and explains why it is odd, matching the style of multimodal GPT-4 and far exceeding BLIP-2 and OpenFlamingo, which mostly just caption the literal objects. The model reasons about the scene, it does not merely list what is present.

The chicken-nugget map. Given a meme image arranging fried chicken to look like a world map, with the question "can you explain this meme in detail?", LLaVA explains the visual joke. The point is generalization: none of the 158K training conversations were about memes, yet the instruction-tuned model transfers its grounded-reasoning skill to a totally novel image type, evidence that it learned a general capability, not a narrow template.

pages.title: A new state of the art on science questions
pages.subtitle: 92.53% accuracy, and what teaming with GPT-4 adds

blocks.html: Open chat is hard to score precisely, so the authors also test on a benchmark with definite right answers: ScienceQA, ~21K multiple-choice science questions spanning natural, social, and language sciences, many of which include a diagram or photo that you must read to answer. It is a clean, quantitative test of multimodal reasoning.
Fine-tuned on ScienceQA, LLaVA alone reaches 90.92% accuracy, already competitive with the prior best. The headline comes from combining it with GPT-4.

How the ensemble works. LLaVA and GPT-4 are made complementary. The simplest scheme treats GPT-4 as a judge: when LLaVA and GPT-4 disagree, the authors prompt GPT-4 to look at both answers and decide on the final one. Because the two models make different mistakes, having the stronger reasoner arbitrate pushes the combined accuracy to a new state of the art of 92.53%.

Why this number matters. It is the first demonstration that a cheap, open, instruction-tuned multimodal model can not only be chatty but also accurate on a rigorous reasoning benchmark, and that pairing it with a powerful text LLM yields more than either alone. The result legitimized the whole "connect-and-instruction-tune" recipe as a serious research direction, not just a demo.

An ablation worth noting: using the CLIP features from the layer before the last (rather than the final layer) helped. The final CLIP layer is over-specialized toward CLIP's contrastive objective and loses localized detail; the penultimate layer keeps richer spatial information that the LLM can exploit, a small but instructive design choice that later VLMs widely adopted.

pages.title: Why LLaVA changed the field
pages.subtitle: The recipe that opened up multimodal assistants

blocks.html: LLaVA's lasting contribution is less a single model than a reusable recipe, simple enough that thousands of teams reproduced and extended it within months:

items: Synthesize, don't annotate. Use a strong text LLM (GPT-4) plus existing image annotations (captions + boxes) to generate multimodal instruction data for free, distilling a capability the teacher itself lacks.
Connect, don't rebuild. Freeze a pre-trained vision encoder and a pre-trained LLM; train a tiny projection between them. Billions of parameters reused, only a thin bridge learned.
Two-stage curriculum. Align the visual-to-text bridge first on captions, then instruction-tune end-to-end on conversations.
Let GPT-4 grade. Score open-ended visual chat with an LLM judge, a methodology now ubiquitous across VLM and chatbot evaluation.

blocks.html: The lineage. LLaVA stands on CLIP (vision-language alignment), Vicuna/LLaMA (open chat LLMs), and the instruction-tuning lineage of InstructGPT and FLAN, applied for the first time to the multimodal setting. It sits alongside Flamingo (gated cross-attention) and BLIP-2 (the Q-Former) as the three canonical ways to fuse a vision encoder with an LLM, and it is by far the cheapest of the three.

What it influenced. The follow-up LLaVA-1.5 swapped the single linear projection for a two-layer MLP, added academic VQA data, and with only public data set new state of the art across 11 benchmarks, all trainable in about a day on 8 GPUs. The architecture became the de-facto template for open multimodal models (MiniGPT-4, InstructBLIP, Qwen-VL, and many more), and "LLaVA-style" is now shorthand for the projector-bridges-frozen-encoder-to-LLM design.

The honest limitations. The authors are candid: because the training data is GPT-4-generated from captions and boxes, LLaVA inherits any biases and hallucinations of its text teacher, can confidently invent details not actually in an image, and struggles with fine-grained recognition and reading dense text (OCR). It is a research artifact, not a deployed product. But as a proof that open, instruction-tuned multimodal assistants were possible and reproducible, LLaVA is one of the most influential vision-language papers of its era.
